guide.title: Hunts Point, the Bronx: Food Markets, Waterfront Parks and THE POINT
guide.intro: Hunts Point is a Bronx peninsula of 690 acres, in Bronx Community Board 2, with the ZIP code 10474. In 1874 New York City, which at the time included only Manhattan, began to annex sections of the Bronx; Hunts Point, originally part of West Farms in what was then lower Westchester County, became the newest part of New York City. Three food markets stand on the peninsula — the Hunts Point Cooperative Market, the New York City Terminal Produce Market and the New Fulton Fish Market — and NYC Parks holds properties across it, among them Joseph Rodman Drake Park & Enslaved African Burial Ground, Barretto Point Park, Hunts Point Riverside Park and the Tiffany Street Pier. THE POINT CDC works from 940 Garrison Avenue, under the strapline "Developing Leadership in Hunts Point Since 1994."

sections.heading: Parks and the waterfront
sections.body:
The Parks properties along the water anchor the peninsula. Hunts Point Riverside Park, where Lafayette Av reaches the Bronx River, was the first section of the South Bronx Greenway to be built; Majora Carter spearheaded it, and NYC Parks calls it a gateway to the revitalized Bronx River and a major connector to the Bronx River Greenway. Barretto Point Park, opened in 2006, looks out to North and South Brother Islands, which are closed to the public. The Tiffany Street Pier lies immediately west of that park and predates it, though NYC Parks classes the pier as a Waterfront Facility rather than a park.

Joseph Rodman Drake Park & Enslaved African Burial Ground is on Oak Pt. Ave. bet. Hunts Pt. Ave. and Longfellow Ave. Three smaller Parks properties sit inside the street grid: Hunts Point Playground on Spofford Av, whose historical sign carries the fullest NYC Parks account of the neighborhood's past; Barretto Park on Barretto St, a separate property from Barretto Point Park despite the shared name; and Julio Carballo Fields on Manida St, named for the founder of the Carballo Youth Baseball League.

sections.heading: The markets, THE POINT and the peninsula's past
sections.body:
Wikipedia's history of Hunts Point names the Wecquaesgeek, a Munsee-speaking band of Wappinger people. NYC Parks' historical sign at Hunts Point Playground carries the later record: the annexation of 1874, the Fox, Tiffany and Leggett landowners, and the acquisition, building and successive restorations of the playground site between 1929 and 2015.

Two buildings stand on Lafayette Avenue. The American Bank Note Company Printing Plant, Gothic-inspired and built between 1909 and 1911, has been a New York City landmark since 2008; it holds a charter school and offices of the Human Resources Administration, and is one to look at from the street. Corpus Christi Monastery houses a Dominican community of cloistered contemplative nuns, founded in the 1890s.

Three food markets occupy the peninsula: the Hunts Point Cooperative Market, the New York City Terminal Produce Market and the New Fulton Fish Market. Wikipedia describes the Cooperative Market as a 24/7 wholesale facility with its own Hunts Point Department of Public Safety of about 45 NYC special patrolmen.

THE POINT CDC works from 940 Garrison Ave., with a second address, its Riverside Campus for Arts and The Environment, at 1391 Lafayette Ave. It runs the Hunts Point Fish Parade & Arts Festival, an annual June event whose 20th anniversary it marked in 2023 under the theme "Rooted Visions." Its own neighborhood history names the Hunts Point Palace among the clubs and dance halls where jazz musicians played, recalls casitas and community gardens and the graffiti "Que Viva Puerto Rico Libre" in the 1970s, and calls the Spofford Juvenile Center "a symbol of pain, abuse, corruption, and neglect."

Bronxlandia, at 910 Hunts Point Avenue, describes itself as a live events venue in the South Bronx and offers rehearsal and event space for booking. Boogie Down Grind Café is open Monday to Saturday by its own posted hours, with no Sunday listed.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
The Hunts Point Avenue station is at Hunts Point Avenue and Southern Boulevard, in the Longwood and Hunts Point neighborhoods of the Bronx, and the 6 serves it. It opened on January 7, 1919. Squire Vickers designed its mosaic friezes, in blue, grey and beige with pale pink, and the large identifying plaques show "H P"; the platform columns are dark green I-beams. The station has been ADA-accessible since November 18, 2014, when three elevators were installed at a cost of $17.8 million.

The Longwood Avenue station is at Longwood Avenue and Southern Boulevard in the Longwood neighborhood of the Bronx. Wikipedia's Hunts Point article lists it among the subway stations serving Hunts Point.

That article also lists bus routes serving the neighborhood: the Bx5, to Co-op City and Bay Plaza Shopping Center via Bruckner Boulevard and Story Avenue; the Bx6 and the Bx6 Select Bus Service, to Washington Heights or the Hunts Point Cooperative Market via Hunts Point Avenue; and the Bx46, to Longwood or the Hunts Point Cooperative Market via Longwood Avenue and Tiffany Street. Confirm current service with the MTA before travelling.

faq.question: How do I get to Hunts Point?
faq.answer: By subway, the 6 serves the Hunts Point Avenue station, at Hunts Point Avenue and Southern Boulevard, which Wikipedia places in the Longwood and Hunts Point neighborhoods of the Bronx. The station opened on January 7, 1919 and has been ADA-accessible since November 18, 2014, when three elevators were installed at a cost of $17.8 million. The Longwood Avenue station, at Longwood Avenue and Southern Boulevard in the Longwood neighborhood, is also listed among the stations serving Hunts Point. Wikipedia's article on the neighborhood lists the Bx5, the Bx6, the Bx6 Select Bus Service and the Bx46 as bus routes serving it; confirm current service with the MTA.

faq.question: What parks are in Hunts Point?
faq.answer: Joseph Rodman Drake Park & Enslaved African Burial Ground, on Oak Pt. Ave. bet. Hunts Pt. Ave. and Longfellow Ave.; Barretto Point Park, on Viele Ave. bet. Tiffany St. and Barretto St., 12.22 acres and opened in 2006; the Tiffany Street Pier, at Tiffany St. at Viele Ave.; Hunts Point Riverside Park, on Lafayette Av bet. Edgewater Rd and the Bronx River; Hunts Point Playground, on Spofford Av bet. Faile St and Hunts Point Av; Barretto Park, on Barretto St bet. Randall Av and Spoffard Av; and Julio Carballo Fields, on Manida St bet. Spofford Av and Lafayette Av.

faq.question: What are the Hunts Point markets?
faq.answer: The Hunts Point Cooperative Market, the New York City Terminal Produce Market and the New Fulton Fish Market. Wikipedia describes the Cooperative Market as a 24/7 wholesale facility with its own Hunts Point Department of Public Safety of about 45 NYC special patrolmen, and records a January 2021 strike there by over 1400 workers in support of a $1-per-hour wage increase and a $0.60 hourly increase for healthcare benefits — the first strike at the market since 1986. The New Fulton Fish Market opened on November 14, 2005 at a cost of $85 million.

faq.question: When is the Hunts Point Fish Parade & Arts Festival?
faq.answer: It is an annual June event run by THE POINT CDC, whose 20th anniversary the organisation marked in 2023 under the theme "Rooted Visions." Check THE POINT CDC, at 940 Garrison Ave., for the current year's date.

faq.question: What is THE POINT CDC, and where is it?
faq.answer: THE POINT CDC is a community development corporation at 940 Garrison Ave., whose strapline reads "Developing Leadership in Hunts Point Since 1994." Its posted hours are Monday to Friday, 10:00 am to 6:00 pm, with Saturday and Sunday closed, and it has a second address, the Riverside Campus for Arts and The Environment, at 1391 Lafayette Ave. It runs the Hunts Point Fish Parade & Arts Festival. Its neighborhood history names the Hunts Point Palace among the clubs and dance halls where jazz musicians played, recalls casitas and community gardens and the graffiti "Que Viva Puerto Rico Libre" in the 1970s, and calls the Spofford Juvenile Center "a symbol of pain, abuse, corruption, and neglect."

photos.title: The brick front of the American Bank Note Company Printing Plant
photos.description: A long red-brick industrial building running away along a street corner under a blue sky with thin cloud. The nearest bay is a tall blank-sided block of dark brick; along the front, brick piers divide the bays, and each of the upper floors carries a wide arched window filled with many-paned steel sash, with rectangular banks of the same glazing on the floors below. Further along the block a square brick tower with a crenellated top and a tall arched opening rises above the roofline, and two white antenna panels stand on the roof nearer the camera. A row of cars is parked along the kerb, a white van and a grey sedan are on the roadway, and young street trees, a red parking sign and a black steel door reached by concrete steps stand along the sidewalk.
photos.author: Jim.henderson

places.name: Barretto Point Park
places.address: Viele Ave. bet. Tiffany St. and Barretto St., Bronx, NY
places.summary: An NYC Parks property on Viele Ave. between Tiffany St. and Barretto St., carried as X307 and 12.22 acres, opened in 2006. North and South Brother Islands are visible from it; the islands themselves are closed to the public.

photos.title: The central lawn at Barretto Point Park, looking towards the water
photos.description: A broad mown lawn, flecked with small white clover flowers and mower stripes, sloping gently away from the camera on a bright summer day. Leafy trees and shrubs close in along the left edge, and a branch in full green leaf hangs across the top right of the frame. A line of trees runs along the far side of the grass, with a footpath, a bin and pale seating visible beneath them at the left, and a metal railing along the right. Beyond the trees the ground opens onto flat water, with a low far shoreline of buildings on the horizon under a blue sky streaked with thin white cloud.
photos.author: Peter Greenberg

places.name: Tiffany Street Pier
places.address: Tiffany St. at Viele Ave., Bronx, NY
places.summary: An NYC Parks property at Tiffany St. at Viele Ave., carried as X304 and 4.23 acres and classed as a Waterfront Facility. The sole facility Parks lists on it is fitness equipment. It is a recreational space that predates Barretto Point Park, which lies to its immediate east.

places.name: Hunts Point Riverside Park
places.address: Lafayette Av bet. Edgewater Rd and the Bronx River, Bronx, NY
places.summary: An NYC Parks property on Lafayette Av between Edgewater Rd and the Bronx River, carried as X336 and 0.43 acres. NYC Parks lists barbecuing areas, fishing, kayak/canoe launch sites and Wi-Fi hot spots here, and describes the park as a gateway to the revitalized Bronx River, a major connector to the Bronx River Greenway, and a home to kayakers, canoers, and paddlers from across the city — a site once an illegal dumping ground, since transformed into a waterfront oasis, with a pier for fishing, a kayak and canoe launch, and a spray shower and playground that take the shape of built-in canoes. Its Parks Vital Signs give a Park Condition Score of 91, recent investment of $754K and 98 mapped trees.
places.history: Construction began in 2004 and was completed in May 2007, making this the first section of the South Bronx Greenway to be built. Majora Carter spearheaded the park, and first envisioned the greenway in the late 1990s as part of a $1.25 million federal transportation grant application. The park is the 2009 Silver Medalist of the Rudy Bruner Award for Urban Excellence, whose award page says the park is now a riverfront oasis with safe access to the river for the first time in over 60 years.

photos.title: Boat-shaped forms around the spray fountain at Hunts Point Riverside Park
photos.description: Three boat shapes moulded in concrete sit on a pale concrete pad under heavy tree shade. On the left is a rowboat with a faded pale blue hull, in the centre a smaller cream-coloured rowboat with bench seats, and on the right a long white canoe. They face a squat carved stone column in the middle of the pad, from whose base a fine spray of water is rising; the concrete around it is stained rust-orange. Low curving walls in ochre and grey stone, set with round studs, ring the space, with planting beds behind them. Black metal benches stand in the shade at either side, a lamppost rises at the back, and an iron picket fence closes off the far edge, with a street, parked cars and low buildings beyond it.
photos.author: RoySmith

places.name: Hunts Point Playground
places.address: Spofford Av bet. Faile St and Hunts Point Av, Bronx, NY
places.summary: An NYC Parks property on Spofford Av between Faile St and Hunts Point Av, carried as X113 and 0.72 acres. Its historical sign carries the fullest NYC Parks account of the neighborhood's past.
places.history: The sign records that in 1874 New York City, which at the time included only Manhattan, began to annex sections of the Bronx, and that Hunts Point, originally part of West Farms in what was then lower Westchester County, became the newest part of New York City. It also names the Fox, Tiffany and Leggett landowners, the acquisition of the site in 1929–30, the playground itself in 1954, a restoration by Blumberg & Butter in 1986, and the Community Parks Initiative in 2015.

places.summary: An NYC Parks property on Barretto St between Randall Av and Spoffard Av — Parks' own spelling of Spofford — carried as X248 and 0.12 acres. It is a separate property from Barretto Point Park.
places.history: Its historical sign records that Coster Street is named for Julia Coster, the wife of Barretto.
